candidates.scan_source: Institutional archaeological site model via Sketchfab
candidates.note: Bronze Age boulder burial, c. 2400–500 BCE, standing at the center of stone circle KE093-032001- near Kenmare. A rounded capstone rests on three supporting stones, forming a small arrangement open to the east; cupmarks and surface striations are visible. “Bronze” describes the period, not the material: the monument is stone and remains in situ.
candidates.source_description: Prehistoric boulder-burial standing in the centre of a stone circle (KE093-032001-) overlooking the Finnihy River, on the outskirts of Kenmare, Co. Kerry. A rounded boulder rests above three support-stones, which form a small chamber-like arrangement open on the eastern side. The boulder rests directly on the support-stones at north and south, and on a small pad-stone above the support-stone on the western side. There is at least one small cupmark and two other holes visible on the upper surface of this boulder.   There are numerous striations or lines visible running across the surface of the capstone.  This type of monument consists of a large boulder or capstone of megalithic proportions, resting on a number of supporting stones, usually three or four in number, which, in most cases, do not form a recognisable chamber structure. Excavations suggest a Bronze Age date for this burial monument (c. 2400-500 BC).  For more information, visit: https://maps.archaeology.ie/HistoricEnvironment/?SMRS=KE093-032002-

candidates.title: Ballybrack Portal Tomb (DU026-030----)
candidates.subject: Neolithic funerary monument

candidates.scan_source: Institutional archaeological site model via Sketchfab
candidates.note: Neolithic portal tomb dating approximately 3800–3200 BCE. The surviving short chamber is formed by tall portal stones, side stones, and a backstone beneath a large sloping roofstone. The monument stands in the Cromlech Fields housing estate at Ballybrack and is also known as Shanganagh Cromlech or Shanganagh Dolmen. The model records the surviving exterior monument and surrounding ground.
candidates.source_description: A type of megalithic (large stone) tomb known as a portal tomb which can be defined as a single, short chamber formed by two tall portal-stones, two sidestones and a backstone. Sometimes a stone between the portals closes the entry. The chamber is covered by a roofstone, often of enormous size, which slopes down from the front towards the rear. Cremation was the preferred burial rite and these date to the Neolithic from 3800 to 3200 BC.  This portal tomb stands today in a low-lying green area on a housing estate called 'Cromlech Fields' in the townland of Ballybrack, Co. Dublin, just off the Shanganagh-Bray road.  Annotated 'Dolmen' on the first edition of the Ordnance Survey of Ireland six-inch map and sometimes called Shanganagh Cromlech or Shanganagh Dolmen. The words dolmen or cromlech are used to a describe a type of tomb with a large flat stone or roofstone resting on upright stones.  For more information, visit: https://maps.archaeology.ie/HistoricEnvironment/?SMRS=DU026-030----

candidates.original_location: Roman cemetery at Valkenburg, South Holland, Netherlands
candidates.attribution: 3D model “Beeldje van een moedergodin uit Valkenburg” by The National Museum of Antiquities (rmo_leiden), via Sketchfab, CC0 1.0. Atrium may serve an optimized derivative.
candidates.scan_source: Institutional cultural-heritage 3D model via Sketchfab
candidates.note: White pipeclay mother-goddess figurine made in a Cologne workshop around 150–200 CE. A smaller male figure at the goddess’s right is interpreted as a worshipper. The complete figurine was recovered from the Roman cemetery at Valkenburg in South Holland; no human remains are represented in the model. National Museum of Antiquities accession h 1941/3.7.
candidates.source_description:
Dit beeldje is gemaakt van witte pijpaarde of terracotta en het stelt een moedergodin voor. Aan de rechterzijde van de godin staat een kleiner mannelijk persoon, die vermoedelijk een aanbidder voorstelt. Het beeldje is gemaakt in een atelier aan de Rudolfplatz in Keulen en dateert uit de periode 150-200 na Chr. Dergelijke beeldjes waren erg populair in de Romeinse tijd en zijn dus in grote getale gevonden in Nederland. Het beeldje is afkomstig uit het grote Romeinse grafveld in Valkenburg (ZH) en is daarom compleet bewaard gebleven. 

**Details**
Inventarisnummer: h 1941/3.7
Afdeling: Nederland Romeinse tijd
Vindplaats: Nederland, Zuid-Holland, Katwijk, Valkenburg
Materiaal: aardewerk
Afmetingen: 18,5x7,4x4,9 cm
Periode: 150-200 na Chr.
Verwerving: aankoop 1941 maart

candidates.title: Isis-Aphrodite figurine (multispectral)
candidates.subject: Domestic protective image of Isis-Aphrodite
candidates.current_location: Kelsey Museum of Archaeology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA
candidates.original_location: House at Karanis, Egypt
candidates.source_institution: Kelsey Museum of Archaeology, University of Michigan
candidates.attribution: 3D model “Isis-Aphrodite figurine (multispectral)” by Kelsey Museum of Archaeology (Kelseymuseum), via Sketchfab, CC BY 4.0. Atrium may serve an optimized derivative; changes include mesh and texture optimization.
candidates.scan_source: Institutional cultural-heritage 3D model via Sketchfab
candidates.note: Small clay figurine of Isis-Aphrodite from a house at Karanis, dated to the first–third century CE. In the anasyromene pose, the syncretic deity lifts her robes in an apotropaic gesture associated with love, marriage, childbirth, and protection. Multispectral imaging identified rose madder in the pink and purple areas, though reconstruction of the original appearance remains interpretive. Kelsey accession 0000.00.6488; 7.1 × 2.1 × 1.5 cm, 19 g. The Kelsey Museum holds the figurine; its current display status is not stated.
candidates.source_description:
Isis-Aphrodite figurine, Roman/Egyptian, 1st–3rd cent CE. Clay, paint; 7.1 H x 2.1 W x 1.5 cm D; 19 g. ID: 0000.00.6488.

Isis-Aphrodite was a syncretic deity of love, beauty, marriage, and childbirth, combining attributes of the Egyptian goddess Isis and the Greek goddess Aphrodite. Here she is in the *anasyromene* pose, lifting her robes to ward off evil. Found in a house at Karanis, we might imagine a child bringing this object home for good luck. The figurine preserves some original color: purple robes and pink crown. These are difficult colors to interpret because both can be created using different pigments and techniques. Multispectral imaging revealed that this pink was created using rose madder pigment while the purple was rose madder combined with black pigment.

For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.6488

To see multispectral bands, open the inspector:

* **Visible Light** > Final render
* **Ultraviolet-induced visible luminescence (UVL)** > Sheen
